newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: BIS plans to sign up emerging country members.
newsitem.headline: BIS plans to sign up emerging country members.

text.p: Plans for the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) to expand its membership to include emerging economic powers in Asia and Latin America are nearing their climax.

Central banking sources said an increase in the number of shareholder central banks from the present 32, which has been in preparation for several years, could be approved by the BIS board at its next meeting on September 9.
"The expansion of the membership is an important symbolic act because it shows the BIS is not just European," one international monetary source said.

The BIS, a central bank for central banks, was founded in 1930 to deal with the settlement of German reparations after World War One with six members, Britain, Germany, Belgium, Italy, France and Japan.

The bank, based in the northern Swiss city of Basle, has expanded over the years. But it remains predominantly European, with Japan, the United States, Canada, Australia and South Africa the only current members from elsewhere in the world.

Central banking sources said the planned increase in membership would not only mark a shift in power away from Europe, but also assure the future authority and legitimacy of BIS, the world's oldest international financial institution.

The BIS is not saying who might join. A Reuters survey of 15 potential new members, including Russia, India, Malaysia, Singapore, Hong Kong, Brazil, Chile and Venezuela, revealed only that the Bank of Korea was in talks about joining.
"Our bank has been interested in joining the BIS membership and is now in the process of discussing the details with the BIS," a spokesman for South Korea's central bank said.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said it would be happy to consider BIS membership if invited.

The BIS's daily workings are unlikely to change much with the expansion, since many emerging countries have taken an increasing role in its activities since 1994, when the European Monetary Institute (EMI) was created.
The founding of the EMI, an embryo European central bank, has given the BIS the impetus to widen its international role.
The BIS provides a wide range of services to central banks, including research of monetary issues and banking operations that assist central banks in managing reserves.

But it is the BIS's function as a gathering point or home-from-home for central bankers that makes it stand out from other economic institutions, such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD).

It is particularly valued by the central bank governors of the Group of 10 rich industrial nations and other countries who hold meetings there 10 times a year to discuss topical issues and swap views.
The challenge will be to retain the informal and confidential club-like nature of discussions, when new members join.

"We don't want to become an IMF. That makes it difficult to decide to whom you say yes and to whom you say no," Wim Duisenberg, president of the Dutch central bank and chairman of the BIS, told Reuters in June.
The BIS's expansion coincides with efforts to create a forum for central bank cooperation in Asia, a development that the Basle-based institution encourages.
BIS general manager Andrew Crockett told Reuters in June there was plenty of room for regional groupings, with the BIS forming a type of umbrella organisation.
The BIS is unique at the international level in being owned and controlled by central banks rather than governments.

Through wars and crises, the BIS has provided a forum for cooperation where central bankers can meet in confidence away from public gaze and build up relationships that prove invaluable at times of crisis.
